After multiple iterations, I led efforts to unify fragmented interface styles. Improved modal behaviors and exception flows (e.g., failed approvals, time restrictions) to enhance usability and maintain visual consistency.

Online Policy Loan Application

Simplified the application process and enhanced visual clarity. Designed a clear guidance mechanism to assist users. Post-launch usability testing showed strong satisfaction, along with an increase in actual applications.

Worklink Website Redesign

Redesigned this SaaS site to increase trial sign-ups and lower bounce rate. Refined IA and UI based on internal insights, adding multilingual support for global users.

Through different pursuits, 
I uncover who I might become.

Design culture shake

I led a design lecture event, inviting international designers to share their work. We used Gather to create culturally themed virtual rooms for a more immersive experience. I also hosted the event to keep it engaging and enjoyable.

I acted as the host of the event to make sure everyone had a good time.

BOOK CLUB

Inclusive Design

I invited designers of different products to read the research content of Google Material Design, and share the concept and examples of inclusive design with the design team.

I shared adjusting Grade for Mode to understand the difference in weight in light and dark modes.

WORKSHOP

Reborn lecturer

I lead workshops to assist non-UX practitioners and students to experience the design thinking process.

Sharing design experience is a different thing than projects, which also makes me constantly reflect on myself.

PODCAST

Podcast：Fintech Store  

On Cathay Pacific's self-run podcast, I share what difficulties I have encountered in the past experience of changing jobs and how to improve.

Recording needs to pay more attention to the rhythm of your speech, which is very new.

Design is inspired by the ordinary moments 

— work and life go hand in hand.

About

About

Hi, I'm Rachel.

I currently lead design at Codi. Previously I've worked at Brilliant, RaiseMe, and Google, and earlier co-founded Secret Mumbo where two iMessage games shipped to over 1M downloads at launch.

I tend to see the world as combinations of parts working in harmony. Great films bring together visuals, sound, and a point of view. Great teams bring together people who play to each other's strengths, support each other's growth, and care as much about how they work as what they ship.

When I'm not designing, I can be found drumming in bands, working through my Letterboxd watchlist, or snuggling with my cat, Koko 🐈‍⬛. I also recently illustrated a children's book.

Designing VSCO’s Capture Experience

Aspiring pro photographers want better-looking photos, but physical cameras feel expensive and hard to learn. Phone camera apps are convenient, but they don’t teach pro control or deliver a consistent “look” quickly.

We saw an opportunity to make Capture an on-ramp: give creators a pro-feeling camera experience with real-time presets and learnable controls, then seamlessly bring them into VSCO’s editor and eventually Pro.


IMPACT
Exceeded month-one targets: 150K downloads · 45% D1 retention · 4.5★ rating

Shipped: real-time presets · manual controls (Exposure / ISO / Shutter Speed / WB / Flash) · Bloom/Halation (progressive tuning) · zoom • gallery · onboarding

Codified capture-mode patterns into the design system (validated in usability tests)
PRODUCT

VSCO Capture (Camera App)

ROLE

Product Strategy + Roadmap
Interaction + Visual Design
Prototyping
Usability Testing + Beta Validation
Design System Contributions

TEAM

1 PM · 3 Engineers · QA · UXR Partner

DATE

2024-2025

The messy reality

We were building 0→1 with unclear requirements, a short timeline, and Apple Camera API constraints that limited exposure/shutter/lens behavior. The work wasn’t just designing screens—it was defining what V1 had to prove, then building a system (controls, gestures, states, and feedback) that could ship within those constraints.


Three decisions that shaped the product

1) “Simple first” beats “everything upfront”


Question: Do aspiring pros want all controls visible for speed, or a cleaner interface that helps them start fast?

I ran a concept test on layout preference + learnability. Users consistently preferred a clean surface with progressive depth, not a control-heavy cockpit. That became the core principle: simple by default, advanced when ready, with guidance that stays out of the way.


Concept A: Pro Speed (Cockpit)


Concept B: Aspiring Pro (Guided)


2) Reduce hunting by grouping around how people think


Early explorations split features into more buckets. In usability tests, that increased friction — not because controls were hard, but because users couldn’t find them.

I merged effects into the manual controls to avoid a separate “Effects” section at launch, which reduced navigation and made key controls easier to find. Usability validation confirmed the new grouping kept advanced features discoverable.


3) Ship clarity and polish before advanced complexity


Across usability testing and MVP validation, aspiring users rarely reached for ISO during shooting—it wasn’t part of their current workflow. Given API constraints, I recommended prioritizing the core value — presets, foundational controls, and interaction quality — and sequencing advanced controls behind a roadmap rather than forcing them into MVP. Launch feedback validated this direction: users highlighted ease-of-use and presets as the primary value.


Outcome

We shipped the MVP and exceeded month-one goals:
‍150K downloads, 45% Day-1 retention, 4.5 rating.


Design system contributions


To make Capture feel “pro” without clutter — and keep the ecosystem coherent — I introduced reusable patterns (validated in usability tests) that are now part of the design system:


Viewport-first controls: floating toolbar overlays the viewfinder instead of growing panels.

Progressive depth: advanced effects use a “Strength-first” drill-in with secondary sliders in a drawer.
Capture-mode conventions: white balance presets + one-tap reset optimized for real-time shooting.


Next steps


After launch, I led the next learning loop to shape iteration priorities:


Ran an unmoderated usability study on preset management + control persistence
Partnered on moderated interviews with users who tried and didn’t return

Facilitated an insights workshop to translate findings into a prioritized roadmap

The Job of Your Portfolio

As someone who has been on both sides of the design world, creating designs and hiring those who create them, I've seen my fair share of portfolios. Thousands, in fact. And if there's one thing I've learned, it's that many designers misunderstand the primary role of their portfolio.

Typecasting Designers

What happens when we typecast a designer? We find ourselves in a world where a brilliant UX designer is passed over for an e-commerce website design role because their portfolio is filled with healthcare app designs. Or where a graphic designer with a flair for typography is rejected for a logo design role because they don't have logos littered across their CV.

Don't Be Perfect, Be Human

In a world where perfection is often overvalued, it's crucial for us designers to appreciate the merit of embracing imperfection. This post examines the significance of acknowledging our human authenticity and uniqueness in design, and how this approach can lead to more profound and engaging product designs that strike a deeper chord with users.

Influence That Travels

The best measure of a senior designer isn't the org chart, it's how far the work reaches and how many people want to build with you. My patterns get adopted across teams, my prototypes become the thing everyone rallies around, and my provocations have redirected product strategy.

I run open design office hours because raising the bar for other teams is part of the job, and the partners I've shipped with keep asking to work together again. If you want to talk craft, AI design, or how I approach the work, I'd love to connect.

I'm focused on the hardest, most ambiguous AI and 0-to-1 design problems as a senior IC, at the Principal or Sr. Staff level. With deep experience at companies like Intuit, Twitter, Ancestry, and various start-ups, and a track record of shipping novel products in code, I'm ready for the next hard thing. Howdy, I’m John Wayne, a technically minded Principal Product Designer.

AI and agentic products, shipped in working code, with deep UX and interaction design behind the patterns. I’ve led design teams and directed a design org, and I’m choosing to build. San Francisco. Intuit. Twitter. Ancestry. 16+ years experience.

VIEW WORK

ABOUT JOHN WAYNE

Full-stack craft, hands on.

Hands-on design across a wide range of industries, platforms, and experiences.

I bring the full stack of craft to a product: product thinking, interaction design (UX), visual design, prototyping in code, and research. My approach is data-driven, user-focused, and relentlessly geared toward quality. I'm known for turning complex data into actionable insights, and for setting a high craft bar by example rather than by memo.

Lately I've been most energized by the hardest, most ambiguous problems, including AI. I'm designing agentic experiences where the patterns aren't settled, prototyping them in code, and getting them shipped. I've been trusted to lead teams repeatedly, and I treat that as one more way the work travels, evidence of range and scale, not the headline. The making is where I want to be.

CORE STRENGTH 01

Designing AI Products

My most current and differentiated work is designing AI and agentic products in spaces where the interaction patterns aren't established yet. I define the patterns, pressure-test them fast, and ship. The ones I built at Intuit are now used by 20+ teams.

CORE STRENGTH 02

Product Thinking

One of my superpowers is synthesizing tons of data into actionable insights and ideas. I think about the holistic and long-term possibilities and help deliver on business objectives. I lead through storytelling, close collaboration, and deeply understanding customers.

CORE STRENGTH 03

Craft & Code

A vision is only as good as its execution. I obsess over the craft of interaction and visual design, and I prototype in real code (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, long before AI made it easy) so ideas ship as working experiences, not static screens. I lead complex, ambiguous projects from concept to shipped product alongside my cross-functional partners.

Intuit Intelligence

QuickBooks' conversational AI, from a one-week vision sprint to millions of customers

When leadership needed a coherent vision for conversational AI in QuickBooks, I led a one-week sprint to personally design it. On day three, the CEO decided to present the work at the State of the Company. That provocation became Intuit Intelligence: I defined the interaction framework and experience principles, prototyped where no proven pattern existed, and helped ship it to all QuickBooks customers. The patterns I established are now used by 20+ teams across Intuit.

TurboTax Full Service & Verified Pro

Making the expert the product, from a 0-to-1 marketplace to a Full Service launch

I was the first and only dedicated designer on TurboTax Verified Pro, a 0-to-1 marketplace matching consumers with the right independent tax pro (84 NPS, 21% referral share against a 5.2% forecast). It proved that people wanted the human, not just the software. I turned that insight into a vision for Full Service built on one idea, the expert is the product, prototyped it end to end, and carried it through a reorg. The CEO and Intuit's founder both reviewed it, and it launched to an unprecedented 50% of early-season customers at 2x engagement.

Project Nah gave customers a lightweight, one-touch way to dismiss recommended Tweets and, if they wanted, tell Twitter why. The interaction had to work in the tightest possible screen real estate across Home, Tweet Details, and Notifications. In experimentation it increased personalization feedback by 7.26% and gave people real control over their Home Timeline.

Experience & Background

Across 16+ years in product design I've worked as a Principal Product Designer, Director, and Head of Design, but the through-line has always been the work. Nine years in leading design agencies like Idean/Frog, Stimulant, and Punchcut sharpened my craft, product thinking, and range. Seven-plus years in-house at Intuit, Twitter, and Ancestry put those to work shipping 0-to-1 products, setting the craft bar, and driving the metrics that matter.

The scope of my work is best measured by how far it travels. The interaction patterns I built at Intuit are used by 20+ teams. I helped grow AncestryDNA from under 1M to 22M+ customers and brought Traits to market. And yes, I've built and led design teams (a 3-person team to 13 at Intuit, a 30+ person org at Ancestry). That's proof of trust and range, another way the work reached further.

Featured Articles

The Job of Your Portfolio

As someone who has been on both sides of the design world, creating designs and hiring those who create them, I've seen my fair share of portfolios. Thousands, in fact. And if there's one thing I've learned, it's that many designers misunderstand the primary role of their portfolio.

Typecasting Designers

What happens when we typecast a designer? We find ourselves in a world where a brilliant UX designer is passed over for an e-commerce website design role because their portfolio is filled with healthcare app designs. Or where a graphic designer with a flair for typography is rejected for a logo design role because they don't have logos littered across their CV.

Don't Be Perfect, Be Human

In a world where perfection is often overvalued, it's crucial for us designers to appreciate the merit of embracing imperfection. This post examines the significance of acknowledging our human authenticity and uniqueness in design, and how this approach can lead to more profound and engaging product designs that strike a deeper chord with users.

Influence That Travels

The best measure of a senior designer isn't the org chart, it's how far the work reaches and how many people want to build with you. My patterns get adopted across teams, my prototypes become the thing everyone rallies around, and my provocations have redirected product strategy.

I run open design office hours because raising the bar for other teams is part of the job, and the partners I've shipped with keep asking to work together again. If you want to talk craft, AI design, or how I approach the work, I'd love to connect.

GET IN TOUCH

OPEN TO WORK

Actively looking for my next great team!

I'm focused on the hardest, most ambiguous AI and 0-to-1 design problems as a senior IC, at the Principal or Sr. Staff level. With deep experience at companies like Intuit, Twitter, Ancestry, and various start-ups, and a track record of shipping novel products in code, I'm ready for the next hard thing. Based in San Francisco, open to hybrid, and remote roles. Let's connect!

Originally from Tallinn, Estonia, I come from a family of pattern makers. By the age of 6, I knew how to put together a pair of jeans. Although I studied architecture at Tallinn College of Engineering, I never worked as an architect, aside from internships, including one in Delhi, India in 2004.

FFFFinder is a fast custom-made native macOS app for browsing images and videos without digging through folders.

You point it to one or more folders, and it shows every supported image and video inside them, including everything hidden deep in subfolders, as one clean visual grid. It keeps the original files exactly where they are, but removes the folder maze from the browsing experience.

LayerLoops
2026

LayerLoops is a way to paint with video. Capture a moment and it keeps breathing on your screen; draw bold strokes and the live camera pours through your lines. Stack clips as you go, building a moving collage that feels tactile and immediate—no timelines, no tools, just your finger and motion.

layerloops.com
Form & Field
2026

Form + Field is a self-made photo book based on a simple idea: two frames, one sentence. I photograph ordinary, system-built spaces in different cities and pair images that complete each other. Different places, different years, but often the same rule set. Color that instructs. Geometry that organizes. Hardware that keeps things running. Most people pass by these things. I stop for the unintentional composition.

Unique copy.
ASCII Video Shader
2026

A real-time video shader that transforms footage into ASCII characters, with controls for typography, color, cell shapes, motion, and composition.
Time Stretched
2022-2026

Time Stretched is a visual exploration that delves into the intricate interplay between time, motion, and human perception. Each image in the series freezes a moment in a temporal paradox: the surroundings seem distorted in a chaotic stretch of time, while the central figure remains unchanged amidst the warped fabric of time. This results in elongated landscapes, distorted architecture, and surreal atmospheres, creating a captivating visual atmosphere.

Each image was captured in diverse locales spanning the globe, from the bustling streets of New York to the vibrant landscapes of Tokyo, Barcelona, Bangkok, and beyond. However, within the realm of Time Stretched, geographical distinctions fade into insignificance, as the viewer is transported into an abstract, distorted moment of time. Here, the central character appears alone and suspended in their own temporal bubble, detached from the constraints of place and immersed in the intriguing interplay of temporal paradoxes.

About
What drives a great user experience?

This is the question that inspires me every day as a product designer. It’s why I’m as happy crafting a thoughtful screen as I am creating a research plan, or strategizing a long-term roadmap, or helping a junior designer think through a problem, or thinking up ways to make a product team run more efficiently. I’m a self-starter at heart, and you can count on me to obsess over the whole pie - not just my slice of it. Mmmh - pie.

Some random facts about me:

I have a crippling dependency on chocolate peanut butter icecream.

It’s been said that my handwriting is like a font.

I am a serial dog stalker (including my own).

I was once headed for law school because I loved taking facts and making a case. Now I use those analytical powers to make cases for design solutions.

I work best to the Isle of Dogs soundtrack.

My pandemic cliche was “rare plant day trader”.

Genuinely, I dislike most pants. 👖

Resume
For a different POV, here are some kind words from former teammates:

“I had the privilege to support and manage Bettina during her time at Belkin/Linksys. Without a doubt, she is one of the best critical thinkers I’ve worked with. Her natural curiosity gives her an edge in solving hard problems. We worked in a complicated networking space, yet she is undeterred in seeking the insights she needs no matter how hard it is, or who she needs to speak with. Bettina does not leave any stone unturned which makes her work strong and defensible. She often challenged me and the team to think in unexpected ways – which often resulted in great outcomes.

On top of all that, Bettina is a confident presenter, gifted writer, illustrator and is often seen cheering her teammates along. I truly miss working with Bettina and would work with her again in a heartbeat. If you have the opportunity to work with her, take it.”

Jamie Bolton, UX Manager, Linksys

“Bettina is one of the best designers I've ever had the pleasure of managing and working with. 

When I hired her, she had decided to move to Stockholm in 3 months. I convinced her to come work for us for at least 2-3 months since she had blown me away in the interview process. I thought I was getting a star on my team and I got a superstar. She's amazing at asking the right questions to get to the why, brainstorming creative solutions, and creating phenomenal user experiences. Her attention to detail and ability to design user interfaces is incredible.

Her superpower is injecting delight in every design she produces, and it sets her apart! She's wonderful to work with: smart, fun, funny, proactive, committed, empathetic, energetic, and kind! I cannot wait until our paths cross again - I'd hire her again in a heartbeat (and hope I get to soon)!”

Gabrielle Bufrem, Head of Product, Little Otter Health

I also have a passion for mentoring fellow (and future) designers.

Are you a new designer, wondering how to position yourself for your first job? Or do you already have experience, and are wondering what’s next? Or maybe you’re wondering how to make a great portfolio? Or how to strategize that nerve-wracking whiteboard challenge?

Somewhere along my meandering design journey, I’ve gained a good amount of insight - mostly the hard way. I’d love to talk about it with you. Go ahead and book some time with me on ADPList.

But enough about me,
tell me about you.

Have an interesting story? Need advice? Have an outrageous idea to share? I’m all ears, and would love to connect.

Game changing the pediatric mental health space

Here's an understatement: raising kids isn’t easy. Finding the support you need when challenges arise is even harder. Little Otter Health already had an incredible, supportive care team -- but were looking for someone to design an on-boarding flow that set everyone up for success.

Being the first design hire meant figuring out on-boarding, the patient intake process, and an intuitive dashboard, all while being deliberate in the research/data/problem-focused design process precedents I was establishing. My work included designing assessments that helped parents understand their child's distinct strengths, using brand, copy, motion in support of a calm, trust-building experience.. and, most important of all, contributing to a lot of otter puns.

Want to see how it ended up? See the mobile app here and more about Little Otter Health here!

Sole product design lead

Collaboration, Research, Strategy and Decision Making, Interaction Design, IA, Wireframing, Prototyping, Usability Testing, Copy

Designing between worlds.

I'm Yuhui Qi, a product designer working between systems and people, technology and culture. The most interesting problems live between worlds, and I turn complex ideas into products that feel clear, useful, and human.

8+ years · 0 → 1 · 3M+ users · product leadership

Before design came systems.

I started in chemical engineering, where I learned to think in systems—structure, constraints, dependencies, and cause and effect. At Parsons, Design and Technology introduced me to another way of seeing: people, behavior, interaction, culture, and expression. Product design became the place where both ways of thinking could coexist.

B.E. Chemical Engineering
Zhejiang University of Technology · Hangzhou, China

MFA Design and Technology
Parsons School of Design · New York, USA

Built from zero to scale.

I've spent most of my career turning ambiguity into something real—first by building products, then by helping them grow, and eventually by shaping the direction around them. As a founding product designer, I took consumer products from early ideas to launched experiences—defining the product as much as designing it. As those products grew, the challenge changed: from making something work to making it clear, scalable, and useful for millions of people. Today, as a Head of Product Design, I work across product direction, systems, and the conditions that help teams do better work.

Head of Product Design
Legacy Dept · 2025 — Present

Product Designer / Digital Designer
Honest Media · 2023 — 2025

Founding Product Designer

McCann Worldgroup · 2020 — 2021

Beyond the product: a wider practice.

Product is my core practice, but it is not the whole of my practice. Product taught me how to make things useful; culture taught me why people care. That wider practice moves through brand, visual culture, experimental design, and art and technology.

The next product thinks with you.

The next boundary I'm interested in is between human judgment and machine intelligence. I want to build intelligent products that use AI as product behavior, not just as a feature—products that help people understand information, make better decisions, and stay informed and in control. The direction is simple: human judgment remains central, while AI expands what a product can notice, explain, and help us do. Designing for shared intelligence.

Previously led design on NotebookLM and contributed to AI efforts across Google Labs including Search (AI Overviews), Gemini, and more. I also shoot photo and video for brands like Coachella, GoPro, and Rivian.

Personal intelligence platform. An AI-native, voice-driven app that delivers deeply personalized content, shaped entirely by your context, intent, and habits.

CO-FOUNDER

CURRENT

I led design for NotebookLM, shaping the product’s core UX, brand identity, and overall user experience from concept to launch.

DESIGN LEAD

UX DESIGN + IDENTITY

🏆 AWARD WINNER

I supported Gemini during its earliest days (when it was still Bard), working closely with a small team to shape some of its foundational features.

UX DESIGN

2 PATENTS

UX DESIGN

VISUAL DESIGN

Shot pre-launch Pixel photos, one of my dog ended up on stage at the keynote, in AT&T stores, and on billboards nationwide.

PHOTOGRAPHY

MARKETING

Shaped the brand identity and visual direction of Veso, an aperitif crafted and bottled in San Francisco, built as a simple, scalable system.

CREATIVE DIRECTION

Voice Interaction

I’ve spent much of my career exploring voice, designing interactions across Google Assistant, YouTube, and the Next Billion Users team. That work took me to places like India, Indonesia, and Brazil, where I researched voice usage and helped create a playbook for emerging markets.

​

I also partnered with IDEO and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation on voice-led initiatives to expand digital literacy.

NBU Voice Playbook

Authored a voice playbook focused on best practices for designing in and for emerging markets.

Photography and Videography

Alongside my design work, I capture photo and video across a range of creative needs, from launch content for Google Pixel (featured on stage at the keynote) to social campaigns for brands like GoPro, Coachella, and Rivian. While design has recently taken precedence, I remain deeply passionate about content creation.

pages.title: Core Motion · AI Garage
pages.text:
Skip to content
Home
CORE MOTION
The spark
The signpost
What I built
Under the hood
Closing thoughts
ALL PROJECTS
PixelAgent
Aura
Core Motion
Prototype · 2 hours with AI
SIDE PROJECT — 01
What if this
signpost
moved with my phone?

As a designer I've been shifting my attention from how a thing looks to how it feels, and the fastest way to feel an interaction is to hold it in your hand.

The light-bulb moment came in San Francisco, under the Sister Cities signpost. One arm pointed to Seoul, my hometown, 5,600 miles away. I thought: what if this whole thing reacted to the gyroscope in my iPhone?

Building a high-fidelity motion prototype like that used to take a week. With AI, I vibe-coded a working Core Motion app in about two hours.

tilt to find the way

THE SIGNPOST
A cluttered sign, pointing home

The Sister Cities signpost in San Francisco stacks two dozen arms on one pole (Manila, Seoul, Ho Chi Minh City, Zürich, Amman), each with a bearing and a distance. It's gloriously busy, and standing under it I kept tilting my head to read the one pointing at Seoul.

The Sister Cities of San Francisco signpost: the cluttered, tilt-to-read object that started it.

“What if this reacted to the gyroscope in my iPhone?”

That single question was enough to start building. Instead of two dozen fixed arms, one big arrow, and instead of moving my head, I move the phone.

WHAT I BUILT
A signpost you steer by tilting

The app drops twelve of the nearest capital cities to Mountain View, CA onto a circular dial, each placed at its true bearing. A single oversized arrow sits in the middle. Tilt the phone and the arrow swings; whichever city it points closest to lights up, and a card names it with its direction and distance.

gyroscope
Tilt to aim. Device motion drives the arrow at 60 fps.
manual
Drag a finger around the dial to swing the arrow by hand.
hybrid
Gyroscope by default; grab the dial any time to take over.

A settings panel tunes the tilt sensitivity so the arrow can feel twitchy or calm, and a haptic tap fires the moment a new city is selected, the small thing that makes a screen feel physical.

UNDER THE HOOD
Just Core Motion and some angle math

A CMMotionManagerstreams device-motion updates sixty times a second. I take the attitude's pitch and roll, convert radians to degrees, clamp them to ±30°, and scale by the sensitivity factor. That becomes the arrow's rotation. The selected city is simply whichever bearing has the smallest angular distance from where the arrow points.

framework
Core Motion + SwiftUI
update rate
60 fps device-motion stream
inputs
attitude pitch + roll, clamped to ±30°
selection
nearest of 12 capital bearings
built in
~2 hours, AI-paired

It's a prototype, not a shipped app: the gyroscope needs real hardware, so it comes alive on a device, not in the simulator.

CLOSING THOUGHTS
Mockups are no longer the starting point

Those two hours changed how I think about design handoff. The gap between idea and implementation has mostly closed.

When a working motion prototype costs an afternoon instead of a week, the static mockup stops being the destination. It becomes the warm-up. AI lets us start from creative experimentation: feeling it in the hand, on day one.

Core Motion · 2024

pages.text:
Skip to content

Hi, my name is

Rafael Conde

I design and make apps and stuff

2026
Retro

I joined the team behind the app Retro as a Design Engineer, one of the few "feel good" apps that still bring me so much joy to use daily.

Download from the App Store
Side Project
Hand Mirror

A Mac app that lives in your menu bar, and when you click on it you get a view from your camera.

Built this in a weekend back in 2020 and it has been a dream side project for me ever since — a small macOS app that people seem to enjoy and it has been featured by the App Store, The Verge, MacStories, 9to5Mac, and others.

I hope it would make my 16 year old self proud!

Download from the Mac App Store
Marketing site
Side Project
Night Knight

I was out on holidays with my family and realized I'd forgotten to bring my kids' night clock, so I built this — it's a night light, noise machine, and wake aid that turns to a different color at a certain time of day.

Free on the App Store
2023–2026
Sketch

I started the year of 2023 by joining the Product Design team at Sketch, an app that has meant so much for me both personally and professionally.

Visit our landing page
Side Project
Thwip

Your portable soundboard, available for iOS and watchOS.

What started as a simple soundboard app for Apple Watch, evolved motivated by playtime with my son — a way to have custom boards for all the Mario sound effects, animal sounds, and quick audio recordings of him saying cute things, that I know won't last long enough.

Download on the App Store
Marketing site
Side Project
Spatialty Coffee

Discover and follow coffee recipes, in spatial computing.

My first foray into visionOS development happened when I was wearing my Vision Pro and got up to make some coffee… made sense at the time.

Download on the App Store
Side Project
Docktor

Preview app icons in the Dock.

Made this small utility to make my workflow slightly more pleasant when designing macOS app icons, simply drag and drop your icon to preview it in the Dock.

Download for free
Side Project
HiDock

A Mac app that lets you set custom Dock settings for when on different displays.

I wanted to have my Dock visible when connected to my large external display, but hidden and smaller when on my laptop, I couldn't believe that there was no way to do that so I built this.

Download for free
2021–2023
Along

I got to scratch "work with friends" off my bucket list when I joined Sam Soffes and Bryn Jackson as their Founding Designer at Along.
The goal was to build the best platform for creators to produce amazing content, engage their community, and make a living.

2016–2020
Netlify

I joined Netlify in 2016 as their first designer and was responsible for designing and scaling our app's UI for the next 5 years.

I’ve also led the 2018's marketing and brand redesign, and helped hire and grow our incredible Product Design team.

Learn more about Netlify
Side Project
Booby Track

Convenient and fun way to keep track of your breastfeeds,
on your iPhone and Apple Watch.

A couple of weeks after our son was born, my partner asked if I could write an app for her to keep track of which boob did she feed our baby with last, and at what time. This is that app.

Download on the App Store
Landing page
Mac OS X
Remastered Wallpapers

Classic desktop pictures modernized in 6K resolution and P3 Color Gamut.

I absolutely love these "classic" wallpapers, and was heartbroken when I realized I couldn't find a high enough resolution for my display, so I tweaked them here and there to bring them back to the modern display technology.

Go to site
2015–2023
Layout

Layout was a podcast about design, technology, and everything else.

For almost 8 years, my friend Kevin Clark and I recorded 364 episodes of what became the most fulfilling and special side project I've ever done.

Give it a listen
Side Project
Break this Safe

An Apple Watch game in which you take advantage of the Digital Crown and haptic feedback to break into a safe.

No longer available to download, as a certain version of watchOS introduced some fatal bugs and I haven't had the time to invest back in it.

Read the case study
In a previous life

WORK PRESENTATIONS ABOUT RESUME CONTACT
Hello, my name is Ryan Breault

I am a systems designer based in Seattle, WA. I studied Communication Design at the University of North Texas. After being introduced to user experience during an internship in Dallas, TX, I've since dedicated my career to solving complex interaction problems at scale.

Over the past decade, I've grown from a trusted design consultant into a staff-level product design leader, partnering with enterprise organizations to transform deep customer insights into elegant, systems-level design solutions.

Comfortable operating across the full design spectrum — from research and wireframing to high-fidelity prototypes and production-ready contributions alongside engineering teams — I bring both craft and strategic clarity to every product challenge.

I'm a tenacious, self-driven designer who thrives in fast-paced, ambiguous environments. I'm proactive about raising the quality of design around me, whether through mentorship, establishing design systems, or championing the adoption of emerging tools like Claude Code, Windsurf, and AI-assisted workflows.

Fluent in a wide range of design and prototyping tools, I communicate product intent through carefully articulated documentation, well-structured design files, and a sharp ability to align cross-functional teams around a shared vision.

Skills
DESIGN
RESEARCH
ENGINEERING
Beyond Design
Cycling

Before design my career had me wrenching at a local bike shop. When I want to detach from the world, you can find me bikepacking across the nearby mountain ranges or dodging cars downtown on my daily commute.

Painting & Drawing

My love for design was born from my desire to become a fine artist. While I don’t need to get the brushes out to do my day job, you can still find me dabbling in oil paints and watercolors on the side.
Check out some of my work.

Ice Hockey

From an early age I grew up playing hockey, it was the only way to stay cool in the heart of Texas. I love all things hockey and continue to play in adult leagues in the Seattle area.

February 2025 — Current

PandaDoc
Staff Product Designer

PandaDoc is the platform where proposals, quotes, and contracts get created, negotiated, and signed. I joined to help answer the question every software company faces right now: what does this product become in the age of AI?

I drive the AI design strategy for the platform — anticipating where generative document creation, model training, and metadata are heading, and turning that into experiences people trust. Every dot in the story below — design systems, growth, research, scale — turned out to be preparation for this chapter.

Contributions
Drive the AI design strategy for PandaDoc's platform, anticipating industry trends in generative document creation, model training, and metadata
Lead end-to-end discovery and validation initiatives, translating research insights into on-brand product experiences
Partner with product and engineering to take AI concepts from first prototype to shipped feature
What I've learnt
Designing for AI means designing for uncertainty — the interface has to earn trust when the output isn't guaranteed
Working prototypes beat static mockups for aligning teams around ideas that don't exist yet

June 2022 — February 2025

Shares
Product Design Lead

Shares set out to make investing social: a European app where you buy your first stock alongside your friends instead of alone. Fresh off a $40M raise, the company needed design to move as fast as its roadmap.

As Product Design Lead I tied growth, brand, and product into one design strategy — and kept shipping while the company expanded from its UK launch to an EU stock-trading licence.

Contributions
Led the design strategy for growth, turning acquisition and retention opportunities into measurable gains in engagement and conversion
Built a scalable design system that kept a fast-moving product consistent across platforms
Shipped experimental products to hunt for new market fit — including a viral waitlist game built for the European launch
Mentored the design team, raising the bar of its craft while the product raced through releases
What I've learnt
In fintech, trust is the product — every screen carries regulatory and emotional weight
Growth design works when it serves users first; retention follows value, not tricks
Leading a remote team means designing the process as deliberately as the product

May 2020 — August 2023

Impress
Founding Product Designer → Product Design Lead

In 2020 I traded a Moscow tech giant for a Barcelona startup with a bold bet: that straightening teeth could work direct-to-consumer, online to clinic. As the founding product designer, I got the thing designers dream about — a blank page.

Two years in, Impress was heading toward a $125M Series B; by three, design had grown from one person with a Figma file into a team embedded across the company.

Contributions
Built the product from scratch, turning customer interviews and journey mapping into a market-fit direct-to-consumer service
Proposed and designed the company's first patient app, moving routine check-ups to photo-based monitoring with a clinician reviewing every step
Launched the updated main website with a complete acquisition funnel and global localization
Designed a suite of back-office tools for clinic operations, cutting costs
Founded the design department: hired, mentored, and grew the team
What I've learnt
As a founding designer, strategy and execution are the same job — you switch between them hourly
Learned to navigate a global market where healthcare, retail, and tech expectations collide
Discovered how to build processes non-product teams actually adopt rather than tolerate

March 2017 — August 2020

Yandex
Senior Product Designer

Yandex — the tech giant behind Russia's search, maps, and voice assistant — is where I learned what scale really means. I helped found the mobile branch of Yandex.Market, its e-commerce flagship.

That branch's revenue grew several-fold and it became the nucleus of the whole e-commerce unit. Along the way I went from designing screens to steering the mobile design department — and stepped on stage to tell the story.

Contributions
Led the relaunch of the Yandex.Market mobile app, driving a 40% increase in user acquisition and a jump in store ratings
Integrated voice-assisted shopping, boosting e-commerce transactions by 20%
Improved the parcel receiving flow, lifting customer satisfaction by 15%
Built a company-wide system for collecting user feedback that sharpened service responsiveness
Represented Yandex as a speaker at Russian Internet Week (RIW), presenting the product relaunch strategy
What I've learnt
Asking the right questions matters more than having the right answers — that's how real user needs surface
Became fluent in customer interviews, from screening to customer development
Learned to test with real service users and let their data shape the prototype
Found my public voice — presenting ideas to large audiences became a tool, not a fear

May 2016 — March 2017

Rambler Group
Product Designer

Rambler is one of Russia's biggest web portals, a holding whose media services reach millions of readers every day.

Always drawn to a bigger challenge, I moved to this media giant to design at portfolio scale: twelve established services to improve and three brand-new platforms to launch.

Contributions
Improved major media products like Rambler News, RNS, WMJ, Lenta, and Championat — lifting user engagement by 15% and average viewing time by 10%, with a direct boost to ad revenue
Rebuilt and relaunched Ferra and Passion, growing daily active users by 20%
Led the transformation of Letidor, which grew its user base 25% within six months of launch
Built and launched Instamedia, a CMS platform for mobile apps that raised editorial efficiency by 30% and sped up content delivery by 25%
What I've learnt
Learned to run multiple large-scale projects in parallel without dropping quality
Sharpened ruthless prioritisation — the survival skill of a fast-paced media environment
Discovered that pitching an idea well is half of shipping it

April 2016 — May 2016

Zvooq
Product Designer

A two-month sprint at the intersection of my work and my passion: Zvooq, one of Russia's leading legal music-streaming services, needed its catalogue to travel beyond the app — so I helped design the way out.

Contributions
Shipped an embedded player that put Zvooq's music on partner sites across the web, growing the user base 25% through partner platforms
Reorganised the web platform's information architecture, extending user sessions by 20%
What I've learnt
Learned to work hand-in-hand with analytics teams, making design decisions from data
Got a deep, practical grounding in Scrum and agile collaboration

February 2015 — April 2016

Webinar
Product Designer

At Webinar, Russia's leading platform for webinars and online meetings, I was the only designer in the building. Every screen, every flow, every release — mine to own.

That pressure turned out to be the best design education I could ask for: relaunch the flagship, ship a mobile app from zero, and build a second product on the side.

Contributions
Relaunched the flagship streaming service Webinar.ru, increasing user engagement by 30% and cutting churn by 20%
Designed and launched a mobile application from scratch, growing the mobile user base 25% in its first six months
Built we.study, a new platform for organising training sessions for educators and learners
What I've learnt
Learned to work shoulder-to-shoulder with developers and plan around real release cycles
Became adept at user funnels, product metrics, and cohort analysis — design decisions backed by numbers
Discovered how much ownership one designer can carry when there's no one else to hand off to

December 2013 — February 2015

Zelenski (Egencia — Expedia Inc. in Russia)
Product Designer

After years of freelancing, I traded independence for my first product seat: Zelenski Corporate Travel Solutions — the exclusive Russian partner of Egencia, Expedia's business-travel arm.

Nine travel services, one designer learning fast alongside marketing and engineering. The habits I picked up here — shipping across disciplines, sweating the typography, hitting deadlines — run through everything above.

Contributions
Designed across nine travel services, partnering with marketing and development teams
Helped launch new projects and marketing campaigns that lifted service adoption and engagement
Improved user interaction across existing services, raising experience quality and satisfaction
What I've learnt
Turned self-taught HTML and CSS into production-grade front-end skills
Learned to collaborate with art directors, balancing design coherence with aesthetic ambition
Built a craft foundation in typography and color that carries from print to product

2010 — December 2013

Freelance
Graphic & Web Designer

Every story has a first chapter. Mine started in the music scene: while studying for an engineering degree, I began designing for music artists and production studios — and kept at it until design stopped being a side project and became the career.

This is where I grew up as a designer. I found a niche where my work was genuinely relevant, learned to sell my skills, and watched one finished project bring the next client. And since I was already at home in HTML and CSS, I could take an artist from a first logo to a live website single-handedly — table layouts and all, as the era demanded.

Contributions
Created branding and visual identity for music artists and production studios
Designed release artwork, concert announcements, and media marketing and production materials
Hand-built end-to-end personal artist websites in HTML and CSS
What I've learnt
Learned to sell my own skills — and that finding the right niche is half the sale
Discovered that good work compounds: every delivered project brought the next client
Formed the design-and-build habit that runs through this whole page: if I can design it, I can ship it

I was born and raised in Utica, NY. My Dad worked as a mail carrier for the Post Office. My Mom worked as a Kindergarten Teacher. Growing up they repeatedly told me to get off the computer and go outside. The OG Touch Grass™. I'm glad I did. There's not a ton to do in Utica but there is a ton to eat and the food is definitely better than where you're from.

When I was 13, I got my first job as a dishwasher at REDACTEDDDDD [redacted due to child labor laws]. After that, I made pizzas at a pizzeria, chased kids around as a security guard at an elementary school, and tried to sell mattresses I knew nothing about at a furniture store.
WHAT I DO NOW
Today I'm a Product Designer at Figma ↗ designing AI experiences. Previously, I was the Founding Product Designer at Diagram ↗. Before all of that, I worked as an Engineer at Romanelli ↗ where I learned how to code (thanks, Zac ↗) and how to stop coding (thanks, Webflow).
WHERE I'M AT NOW
Today, I live in San Francisco, California. When I'm not working, you can usually find me with my dog at the beach, the park, or the redwoods.

Impactful, purposeful work with a diverse team of talented people.
I also think the personal computer needs its iPhone moment ↗.

pages.text:
Skip to Content
Amara Hulslander – Principal Product Designer
Home
Case studies
Contact me
LinkedIn
Amazon Alexa+ AI Developer Studio

Alexa+ is Amazon’s voice user interface platform, designed to let third-party brands build conversational skills that customers can use across Echo devices. The goal is to make it possible for any brand to deliver real customer tasks (ordering food, managing accounts, checking loyalty rewards) through voice and touch, without building the underlying infrastructure from scratch.

For each phase transition, I identified what hands off, what gaps exist, and where the current architecture leaves developers without support. That analysis (what the agent can do, where it stops, and what falls to the developer) became the foundation for the platform. Grouping related goals and tasks across the journey reduced workflow phases by 45%.

What I delivered:

45% reduction in API integration workflows

Jobs-to-be-Done / Developer Experience Outcomes

Design system tokens & components

Agent personality specs & SDK guardrails

Product design strategy roadmap

AI-powered prototypes

The Summary

The Alexa+ developer experience was built on a guided, step-by-step setup experience: static flows that required developers to manually manage context, anticipate system limits, and bridge every handoff themselves.

As the platform shifted toward agentic capabilities, that foundation created compounding problems:

Related tasks were scattered across phases, forcing developers to work inefficiently

Each integration path (API, MCP, and Agent Relay) carried different agent behaviors and developer responsibilities

There was no shared model of where the system balanced agent vs human judgment

The Strategy

I focused on an agentic integration experience, enabling developers to provide assets and natural language during onboarding. The agent would audit the information provided in order to infer and scaffold a customer experience. If there were constraint violations between the SDK guardrails and the 3rd party product requirements doc, the agent would flag those for turn-by-turn resolution with the developer.

The tool would quickly move the developer into an experience that combined building and simulation. They would have the ability to preview the customer experience and then dive into the mechanics of how it worked. From there, they could pinpoint parts of the experience that were incorrectly inferred or scaffolded and fine-tune the interaction or data sources.

Zero compounding mistakes

In probabilistic AI systems, small errors amplify downstream. I designed validation checkpoints at every workflow stage so developers caught integration issues before they became embedded in a live skill. 

The trade-off: more gates to maintain, but errors that are invisible until they ship are worse.

Preserve momentum

Sequential dependencies meant developers couldn’t test until setup was complete, couldn’t audit until deployed. I designed parallel workflows so multiple stages could progress simultaneously. 

The trade-off: more complex to architect, but developers no longer waited on upstream stages to resolve before moving.

Autonomy where it’s earned

Not every agent action needed the same oversight. I defined a framework matching oversight requirements to decision weight. Low-stakes actions proceed autonomously, high-stakes ones require confirmation. 

The trade-off: more nuanced agent logic required, but treating all decisions identically makes the system either too slow or too risky.

Story

I'm Olha Bahaieva, a Staff-level Product Designer with 12+ years of experience, but UX/UI wasn't my first discipline. I started in interior design and architecture, learning how people move through physical space on projects like a hotel's hall layout and room wayfinding, designed in 3ds Max.

Physical space carries a different kind of risk than digital design, a mistake can't be quickly patched. That pushed me toward a faster-iterating discipline. I built a design portfolio through 99designs (reaching top-tier status) and Behance, moved into web design, then taught myself UX/UI, later earning a Gold win in Interactive Design at the Indigo Design Awards along the way.

Today, I lead UX/UI at DISH Network and, as a top 3% Toptal designer, create products used by 12M+ people.

Beyond product design, I teach UX/UI to 1M+ learners and founded UX Designers Club, a design community to help other designers grow their careers.

Design Philosophy

I design for business outcomes, not just wireframes — because at enterprise scale, great UX must move metrics. That instinct traces back to interior design: a floor plan either helps people move through a space or it doesn't, and a product either helps people get something done or it doesn't. Same question, different material.

Career

From an early career in visual and interior design, to UX/UI roles across telecom and hospitality in Europe, to leading product design for Fortune 200 scale at DISH Network today — with Toptal's top 3% freelance work running alongside it since 2018. Ten roles, one throughline: turning complex, high-stakes products into something people can actually use. I'm now focused on Staff+ product leadership roles and select freelance partnerships that call for that same range.

I'm Olha Bahaieva, a product designer leading self-service design at DISH Network. My work spans AI-native products, SaaS dashboards, design systems and 0-to-1 startup products across web, iOS and Android. I work with teams in New York and remotely, on full-time roles and project engagements.

Frequently asked questions
Who is Olha Bahaieva?

Olha Bahaieva is a product designer and Lead UX/UI Designer at DISH Network, where she designs self-service experiences used by millions of DISH and Sling TV customers. She was previously Director of Product and Brand Design at VeedoAI and is a Top 3% designer on Toptal.

What kind of product design work does Olha Bahaieva do?

She designs trust-critical product experiences: self-service and account flows, AI-native products, SaaS dashboards and design systems, across web, iOS and Android. Her work ranges from 0-to-1 startup products to features used at enterprise scale.

Which industries has Olha Bahaieva designed for?

Telecom and streaming, AI-native products, SaaS and B2B, financial services, health and wellness, e-commerce and marketplaces, and creator and content platforms. Each industry has its own page with related case studies.

Is Olha Bahaieva available for full-time roles or projects?

Yes. She's open to Staff and Principal product design roles and to fixed-scope project work, such as UX audits, 0-to-1 product strategy and design systems. She works remotely with teams in New York and across the US, on Eastern hours.

How are the results in these case studies measured?

Measured results are stated as facts. Estimates are clearly marked "modeled" or "projected," and each case study explains how the number was calculated, so you can see exactly what was measured and what was estimated.

About
About

Hi, I'm Mengmeng.

Senior Product Designer

I design the moment when a complex system starts to make sense—leading end-to-end product work across healthcare, AI, and operational workflows.

At Vibrant Wellness, I learned to turn dense medical information and high-stakes provider workflows into experiences people could understand and act on. I led research and design across 50+ pages serving 250K+ patients and 4K+ providers, helping drive a 58% increase in monthly traffic within two months of launch.

That work led me toward AI. At AgentX, I moved from simplifying established workflows to shaping a zero-to-one multi-agent product—working with founders and engineering to define how people configure agents, follow delegation, and stay in control of automated work.

I then brought that builder mindset back to the team. I turned my own AI-assisted prototyping practice into workshops and reusable workflows adopted by 10 designers across two teams. The progression matters more to me than any individual tool: understand complexity deeply, build the new interaction model, then help a wider team work differently.

pages.title: AgentX — Mengmeng
pages.text:
Mengmeng
Mengmeng
AgentX
AgentX
Intro
The launch
Solution
Challenge
Research
Design decisions
Team Impact
Product Outcome
Design System
AI-Native
Reflection

AGENTX  ·  2025

Teaching people to trust a team they can't see.
ROLE
Lead Product Designer
TIMELINE
2025
TEAM
1 Product Designer
Engineering
1 PM
1 CEO
SKILLS
Product Design
Product Strategy

OVERVIEW

How do you make an invisible team of AI agents feel understandable and trustworthy?

AgentX is a no-code AI agent platform that enables businesses to build, deploy, and orchestrate AI agents without writing code. It helps teams automate repetitive work through customizable AI workflows, making advanced AI accessible to both tech and non-technical users.

Along the way, I developed the Trust Stack—a design framework that helped the team build trustworthy AI experiences across configuration, execution, and multi-agent delegation in future product development.

AgentX’s Product Hunt launch and a post-launch photo with the CEO and team

LAUNCH INSIGHT
Could people understand what their agent team had just done?

Launch feedback exposed the next UX problem: builders could create a team of agents, but couldn't follow how the agents divided work or reached an answer.

I turned that gap into the next design focus—making multi-agent behavior easier to understand and giving builders stronger reasons to return.

SOLUTION — BUILD
Anyone can build powerful AI agents in minutes. No code. No technical background. Even local restaurant and cleaning business owners can do it.

The entry point had to work for someone who's never touched an API. I designed a single guided flow — LLM choice, personality, skills, knowledge — that reads like filling out a form, not writing a program. This was never the hard part of the product, but it had to be effortless for everything after it to matter.

0.5X
2X
↻

Agent Building flow

SOLUTION — ORCHESTRATE
Building a whole team of agents should feel like drag-and-drop, not engineering.

AgentX's real differentiator wasn't one agent — it was letting non-technical people assemble a team of agents that hand off work to each other, with a manager coordinating the rest. I designed that as a visual, drag-and-drop flow: connect agents, assign one as the manager, done. No YAML, no config files, no orchestration logic to write by hand.

0.5X
2X
↻

Drag and drop Multi Agent flow

SOLUTION — UNDERSTAND & TRUST
Seeing how the team actually works is what makes people trust it.

Once a team of agents was live, “easy to build” stopped being the problem. The real question became: can a person watching this actually follow what their agents just did, and why one agent handed a task to another. I designed the reasoning view specifically to answer that — not as a debug log, but as a plain-language window into how the team just did its job.

0.5X
2X
↻

Multi-agent collaboration unfolding in Chat View

Structured Chat View around a Manager–Sub-agent hierarchy.

Using a familiar organizational model made delegation and task ownership legible at a glance, without asking users to learn a new mental model for how one AI coordinates others.

0.5X
2X
↻

Opening the Reasoning panel to follow the team’s work

Folded detailed reasoning behind progressive disclosure.

The first-glance summary preserves agent ownership, tool usage, and key actions; expanding the panel reveals handoffs and implementation details without overwhelming the default view.

0.5X
2X
↻
0.5X
2X
↻
0.5X
2X
↻

Motion used as an information layer across Chat, Reasoning, and system feedback

Make invisible agent behavior readable through motion.

Chat: status motion makes hierarchy, parallel work, and ownership clear.

Reasoning: key actions stay visible; deeper evidence appears on demand.

Thinking: the AgentX mark signals that the system is working.

CHALLENGE 01
The platform can do almost anything. Nothing should force a first-time user to touch all of it.

The builder covered model selection, memory, tools, integrations, and deployment. I separated the essential decisions from optional configuration, added useful defaults, and kept advanced controls one layer deeper. New builders gained a clear route to a working agent; experienced builders kept access to the control they needed.

Building flow

CHALLENGE 02
Nobody has a mental model yet for “one AI managing another.” So I borrowed one.

I gave agents roles people already understand, such as Manager and Reporter, and used reporting lines to make delegation legible at a glance. It was not the first direction we considered—the decision came from testing competing structures.

Visualizing delegation through familiar hierarchy

CHALLENGE 03
We showed users everything their agents did. It looked like chaos, not honesty.

The launch exposed a second trust problem: routine agent activity appeared beside the decisions that actually mattered. Instead of removing transparency, I redistributed it. The goal and summarized key actions stayed visible; raw reasoning, tool execution, and references became available on demand.

Raw activity moved out of the main view; meaningful progress stayed visible.

RESEARCH

RESEARCH
Everyone described what they wanted. Almost nobody could describe what was happening.

Across interviews, builders could describe the outcome they wanted but struggled to identify the next setup decision or explain what happened during a run. The repetition showed that this was a structural product gap, not a copy problem.

0.5X
2X
↻
Our audience
8 builders across semi-structured interviews and usability sessions.
RESEARCH
What people said wasn't what they did on screen.

Interviews surfaced low trust; Hotjar showed the behavior behind it. People skipped the reasoning panel and dropped out partway through the long settings flow. That turned a vague concern into two fixable problems: too many decisions upfront and too much undifferentiated activity during execution.

Hotjar Heatmap of V1 reasoning

DECISION & ALIGNMENT
The CEO wanted flexibility. I was worried users would lose ownership.

In design review, the CEO favored a node graph because it gave builders maximum freedom to connect agents, MCP tools, and delegation instructions. I saw a different risk: as teams grew, crossed connections could make it difficult to tell who owned the task or where work would return.

Rather than argue from preference, I turned both positions into working prototypes. We tested the same setup tasks in the flexible node graph and a manager-led hierarchy, alongside lighter structural explorations. The graph worked for small teams, but became slower to read as relationships accumulated. The hierarchy sacrificed some representational freedom in exchange for clearer ownership and delegation.

I brought each round back to the CEO and engineering in a recurring review: prototype, evidence, edge cases, revision. That changed the conversation from which interface someone preferred to which trade-off best supported the product. The team aligned around the hierarchical canvas, and the CEO became one of its strongest advocates.

Prototypes made the trade-off between flexibility and legibility tangible.

TEAM ROUTINE
A reusable product discovery loop

I didn't want the Product Hunt comment thread to be a one-time source of insight — I turned reading it into a repeatable loop: pull user language straight from comments and interviews, group it into real problems versus noise, design and test a few directions against it, validate with users, ship, and start the loop again on whatever surfaces next. I documented this as a living process in Notion rather than a one-off retro, specifically so it didn't depend on me to run it.

A process the team could reuse

Review feedback, identify friction, and test what to improve next.

I documented the loop in Notion so the team could keep improving the product on its own.

PRODUCT OUTCOME
The numbers that moved.

The redesign simplified onboarding, reduced decision friction, and made complex multi-agent workflows easier to understand. After launch, the product signals moved in the same direction as the research: builders reached a working agent more easily and returned to create more.

35% faster agent setup
42% fewer permission-related drop-offs
61% higher first-run success rate
78% of users created their first agent without documentation
3.7× more agents created per active workspace

Beyond product usage, the platform grew organically across a global builder community and supported the company’s fundraising story. I treat these as product-level outcomes: my contribution was clarifying setup, delegation, and execution while the broader team shaped growth and delivery.

The numbers that moved

What builders actually said.
DESIGN SYSTEM
Two component libraries kept a fast-moving AI product coherent.

I built reusable foundations for light and dark themes, then encoded behavior through Figma—not static reference screens.

SYSTEM MECHANICS
Reusable by construction.

Variants, Auto Layout, Component Properties, Variables, and color, type, spacing, and semantic tokens made themes and states consistent.

100+ · Platform
100+ · Chat + JEEVES
Light + dark themes
AI-NATIVE · DESIGN ENGINEERING
From design intent to production behavior.

I’ve expanded my practice from designing interfaces to shipping the product itself. With Claude Code and Codex, I take focused features from concept to implementation, while evolving the design system into an agent-readable source of truth—clear enough for AI to interpret, reuse, and implement consistently.

Working directly in code, often before opening Figma, lets me prototype at product fidelity, test decisions in context, and iterate against real behavior. The result is a tighter loop between design judgment and production: prototype, validate, refine, and ship.

KEY LEARNINGS
Principles for designing trust in systems people cannot fully see.

AgentX reshaped how I think about transparency, mental models, and organizational learning.

01
Transparency needs hierarchy to become trust.

More agent detail created noise. Trust came from connecting the goal, decision, and supporting evidence.

02
Borrow mental models, not interfaces.

Manager–reporter language clarified delegation. Testing revealed which familiar ideas transferred without creating false expectations.

03
Feedback needs somewhere to go.

A repeatable post-launch loop preserved user evidence long enough to influence the roadmap.

04
A framework should outgrow its author.

The Trust Stack mattered when teammates used it independently to make stronger product decisions.

This is just a snapshot of the entire design process.

Reach out for the full story.

Say hello!

About Me

I'm Irene, a UI/UX Designer & Webflow Developer with over 4 years of experience. Originally from Ukraine, I'm now based in Los Angeles, CA.

As an Awwwards and Orpetron judge, I stay updated with the latest design trends to ensure my work is of high quality.

I leverage the power of Webflow to bring your digital vision to life. Whether you need UI/UX design, Webflow development, or a combination of both, I offer a comprehensive suite of services to meet your website's needs.

I believe design can solve problems and improve how users interact with technology. My goal is to create digital experiences that are both functional and enjoyable.

“If there is a site launch happening, you want her on it. I’ve been lucky enough to have her on all my large website projects over the past 3 years. They have been successful because of her contributions! Both as a UX/UI designer and a Webflow developer, her attention to detail is next level. As a Webflow developer, her QA process kills any bugs before they become an issue. But before we get to the development stage, her design decisions are excellent. I rely on her ability to question (and solve) issues within established design patterns and larger systems. I greatly appreciate her willingness to challenge decisions that she sees critical issues with. She is efficient as hell, is a Figma powerhouse user, is constantly learning new skills, and is the best problem solver. I’ve learned a lot from her over our years of working together. I highly recommend Irene for any website project you have.”

Design Lead at Ashandelle

02 • Sep 2024

“I had the pleasure of working with Irene on several critical internal and external UI/UX and website projects, and I can't recommend her highly enough. Irene is an exceptional designer and what sets her apart is her ability to balance strong design aesthetics with deep UI/UX knowledge...all while possessing critical "business know-how". She consistently delivered designs that were not only visually appealing but also intuitive and user-friendly. Her expertise in Webflow allowed for seamless implementation of these designs, resulting in polished, professional websites that exceeded our expectations. …

I would jump at the opportunity to work with Irene again and wholeheartedly recommend her to anyone looking for a top-tier Webflow and UI/UX designer. She's not just a skilled professional, but also a fantastic team player who will undoubtedly add value to any project or firm.”

I love that Irene is committed to continued learning and keeping up with best practices and her knowledge of Figma and Webflow is impeccable. I may have had help with the other sections, but figured I'd drop a little 100% unassisted content just so you can get a feel… you know?

Origin story

I started out in the NYC print Ad scene (working early in my career under my maiden name, Andrea Berry), mastering the art of Spray Mount until my pitch boards were known for perfect centering and zero bubbles (iykyk). One day, a big client wanted some web ads. They’d seen some "moving ones," and, of course, we sent them off with total confidence that the best team in the city was on it. When the door closed, panic ensued as no one in a 3 floor radius had any idea where to begin. I took this as my cue to hit up the Barnes & Noble on 54th and Lex, flipped through the equivalent of "Flash For Dummies", and, yada, yada, yada, my career in tech was born.

After years of extended happy hours and holiday parties that I’m glad never made social media, I came across ITP at NYU, a graduate program that perfectly aligned with my interests in design and building. It’s here that I gained proper skills as a developer and more niche passions for Onigiri and Arduino.

That led to a bunch of interesting gigs like...

Producing an app that let Oxygen Network reality TV fans video chat with the stars, pre-iPhone (we sent the talent a web cam kit!)
Sourcing prototypes for a customizable bobblehead concept 🙂
Doing UI for a startup focused on amateur influencers
Writing the choose-your-own-adventure SMS stories for Universal Studios' Halloween Horror Nights. (I got SO into this. I re-read them recently and they are still super scary!)
etc... you get the idea

My first job in “UX-proper” came from Huge in Brooklyn, a truly design-led shop that was almost too cool at the time.

I eventually landed at Google, where I’ve been since 2014. Yikes.

Yikes, BUT… these last few years have really been exciting. The potential and pace of AI innovation makes me accidentally stay up all night keeping up with the latest. It’s amazing to have the opportunity to define the way people will interact with machines and witness a total shift in what it means to be in design. Mundane work will soon be completely automated, leaving more room for thinking and iterating.

What else? I grew up on Long Island in the town whose name means, "By the mall", spent 15 years in NYC, did a stint in the Bay Area, and am now back on the East Coast. I'm big into swimming, cycling, and hanging out with my dog, Ronnie, and I've been to a weirdly-high number of Rolling Stones concerts... five countries, six states... a few times each!

What else do you want to know?

PS. There's an Easter egg in here that helps you guess the password for protected pages.

A New Way to Work

AI has rewritten how things get done and products get built. My teams are abandoning long research cycles, 20-page requirements docs, and handoffs that leave engineers waiting. That way of working doesn’t fit a world with the current pace of tool evolution.

Though still controversial, I do not use traditional design software other than to provide the very occasional visual direction to the AI coding tool I'm using. Designing natively with code is much more efficient for making updates, maintaining version history, and, thanks to Skills, even making sure designs are pixel-perfect and on-brand.

We are moving faster while preserving the principle that a good AI system should help users build accurate mental models, understand tradeoffs, and retain agency.

With my teams, I’ve found the learning curve to be extremely shallow, allowing designers with little technical background to get on board with this way of working quickly and easily. We develop robust realistic prototypes, use real apis, and can even help with polish of production code.

On the research front, we can now have 100s of participants record themselves using our builds and have AI help with the analysys, surfacing patterns in hours instead of weeks.

Now, we are constantly building tools to help with our own work. A Creative Director agent looks at designs and gives company-specific feedback. Another scans internal communication channels for discussion about a product, generates insights, and lets the team search across topics. I’ve also built an easy way for my team to share regular progress updates by emailing them a suggested list to verify or edit.

For me, “a new way to work” means teams spending less time wrestling with process and tedium, and more time imagining, shaping, and building what’s next.

About
I design enterprise platforms, zero-to-one products, and cross-platform experiences across web, mobile, and immersive tech.
Background

I grew up across Sweden, Sri Lanka, and Kuwait before settling in the UK. I've been designing since I was 16, starting as a self-taught freelancer building websites for agencies and brands while studying at Oxford Brookes University.

That early freelance work led to my first full-time role at Placester, a Boston-based startup where I worked directly with founders on a zero-to-one product. I was the designer, the researcher, and often the frontend developer. That experience set the pattern for the rest of my career: I've always been closest to the work when I can see the full picture, from strategy through to shipped product.

At Litmus

I joined Litmus in 2015 as the second designer. Over five years I helped scale the team from 2 to 12, served as Interim Head of Design for over a year, and led the end-to-end redesign of the platform after a 200x speed improvement in their core testing infrastructure.

One thing that set me apart at Litmus: I wrote production code. Not prototypes. Actual shipped UI in Ruby on Rails, HTML, SCSS, and JavaScript. It gave me a tighter feedback loop with engineering and a level of implementation fidelity that most designers can't achieve from Figma alone. I also built a Chrome Extension (10,000+ users), designed a Slack integration, created the Design Library (which drove a new revenue stream), and led creative direction for Litmus Live, the company's annual conference.

At Meta

I joined Meta in 2020 and have worked across some of the company's most ambitious bets in collaboration and productivity.

On Meta Portal, I led the strategic pivot from a family calling device to a workplace productivity tool. I ran the foundational research that identified what knowledge workers actually need from a secondary screen, then shipped Calendar, proactive notifications, and one-tap meetings. The work exceeded our activation targets and contributed to 22% of Portal's total device sales. I also invented Ambient Coworking with Avatars, a lightweight calling concept using presence detection and avatar representation. Meta filed a patent on the concept, and it was adopted by teams across web and mobile.

On Workplace, I led the design of Event Studio, a broadcast platform shipped to 20,000+ enterprise customers including McDonald's and Nestlé, reaching 12M+ users with 63% retention. I also developed Meta's Future of Work design strategy alongside senior leadership, defining three core principles (Persistent Spaces, Rich Presence, Equitable Participation) that were presented live to over 2,500 employees and adopted as the go-forward direction by product leadership.

On Horizon Workrooms, I defined and delivered a zero-to-one product vision for virtual events in VR. I led a team of technical artists, concept artists, and engineers, presented the vision directly to CTO Andrew Bosworth, and the product was showcased at Meta Connect 2025.

Today I'm a Staff Product Designer at Meta, leading an AI Pod that's redesigning enterprise procurement workflows for 50,000+ employees. I design human-in-the-loop patterns for AI-assisted decisions: review, escalation, audit trails, and the judgment layer that makes AI systems trustworthy at scale.

How I work

I'm a designer who builds. That's been true since I wrote production Rails at Litmus, and it's even more true now. I use Cursor, Claude Code, and Figma Make alongside Figma to move from concept to working software faster than the traditional design-to-handoff pipeline allows. This site, for example, is a Next.js app I built and deployed to Vercel.

I believe the best design work happens when you can hold the full problem in your head: the user need, the technical constraints, the business context, and the team dynamics. My strongest contributions have always been at that intersection, not just the pixels.

A few things I believe in
Good design scales. A strong system helps teams move faster and stay aligned.
Enterprise tools can be elegant. Complexity should never come at the cost of usability.
Zero-to-one work requires curiosity and patience. It's not linear, and that's okay.
Mentorship is part of the job. Sharing knowledge helps grow great teams.
Designed in Figma. Built with Next.js. Deployed on Vercel.
